summary: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a compact data format, and COSE defines how to sign, authenticate and encrypt data in it, plus how to represent cryptographic keys in CBOR. This document gives the structures and processing rules. Together with RFC 9053 it obsoletes RFC 8152.

plainLanguage.summary: COSE defines standard CBOR formats for signed, authenticated, and encrypted data, as well as cryptographic keys. It also specifies how senders and receivers build the bytes that cryptographic checks use.

subtitle: The CBOR structures and processing steps for signatures, message authentication, encryption, and keys.

tldr.problem: CBOR is designed for compact data, but applications also need common structures for protecting CBOR messages and representing their cryptographic keys.
tldr.mechanism: COSE defines CBOR message structures for signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption, along with key structures and the exact data used in cryptographic calculations.

sections.title: What COSE Provides
sections.content:
Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is designed for small messages and implementations. RFC 9052 defines CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE), which supplies structures and processing rules for signatures, message authentication codes (MACs), encryption, and cryptographic keys.

COSE uses CBOR's support for binary values directly rather than converting them to base64 text. This RFC defines message structures and how to form the inputs to cryptographic functions, but it does not define the full algorithm set. Initial algorithms are specified in RFC 9053.

COSE is intended for store-and-forward or offline protocols. An online protocol that needs encryption must first perform an online key-establishment process.
sections.plainLanguage: COSE gives applications shared CBOR formats for protecting data and carrying keys. This document defines the formats and processing steps, while another specification defines the initial algorithms.

sections.title: The Basic Message Structure
sections.content:
COSE messages are CBOR arrays. Their first three elements hold protected headers, unprotected headers, and the content. The content can be plaintext or ciphertext, and it can be detached and carried separately.

After these shared elements, the structure depends on the message type. COSE defines two forms each for signing, encryption, and MACs. The single-party forms are used when the key is already known; the other forms can carry signer or recipient information.

An application can identify a message by context, a CBOR tag, a media-type parameter, or a CoAP content format. COSE_Encrypt, for example, separates encrypted content from the recipient information used to protect the content key.
sections.plainLanguage: COSE messages share the same first three parts: protected headers, unprotected headers, and content. The remaining parts depend on whether the message is signed, encrypted, or authenticated with a MAC.

sections.title: Protected and Unprotected Headers
sections.content:
Every security object has two header maps. The protected map is encoded as a byte string and included in the cryptographic calculation. The unprotected map is not cryptographically protected. Both maps use labels, which can be integers or text strings.

Labels must be unique within each map. If the same label appears more than once, a receiver must reject the message as malformed. When the same label appears in both maps and the message is otherwise accepted, the protected value takes precedence.

Common parameters identify the algorithm, critical parameters, content type, key identifier, and initialization vector. The crit parameter must be protected and lists parameters a receiver is required to understand. A key identifier is only a hint and need not be unique.
sections.plainLanguage: One header map is protected by the cryptographic operation, and the other is not. A receiver must reject repeated labels and use the protected value when a label appears in both maps.

sections.title: How COSE Builds a Signature
sections.content:
COSE_Sign can carry multiple signatures over the same content. COSE_Sign1 carries a single signature. They cannot be converted into one another because the signature calculation identifies which structure is being used.

Before signing, the sender builds a Sig_structure containing a context string, protected headers, any externally supplied data, and the payload. For COSE_Sign, it also contains the signer's protected headers. The sender encodes this array as bytes and passes those bytes to the signature algorithm.

The application defines how external data is formed so that different inputs cannot produce the same byte string and both sides use the same order. A receiver also checks that the signing key belongs to an authorized identity before acting on the message.
sections.plainLanguage: COSE puts the protected information, payload, and any application-supplied data into a defined structure before signing. Both sides must build the same bytes for signature checking to work.

sections.title: Encryption and Message Authentication
sections.content:
COSE_Encrypt0 is for an implicitly known key and has no recipient structure. COSE_Encrypt carries recipient information and can support multiple recipients. Content encryption uses authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD), so the operation can check both encrypted content and additional authenticated data.

COSE also defines COSE_Mac0 for an implicit key and COSE_Mac when recipient information is needed. A MAC can show that content has not changed. With a shared secret or certain static key-agreement methods, it can also help establish who sent the message to another party, but it does not prove the sender's identity to a third party.

Encryption structures use content keys. COSE describes ways to use a shared key directly, wrap a content key, transport it with a public key, derive it through key agreement, or combine agreement and wrapping.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption protects content and can detect changes. A MAC detects changes using a shared secret; in some arrangements, it can also help the recipient identify the sender.

sections.title: Key Objects and Use
sections.content:
A COSE_Key is a CBOR map with a required key-type field. A key set is an array containing at least one key. Applications process keys in a set independently, so a malformed or unsupported key does not prevent processing the others.

Common key fields can identify the key, restrict its algorithm, list permitted operations, or provide a base initialization vector. If a key names an algorithm, the application must check that it matches the algorithm used for the message. The key type must also be appropriate.

COSE is designed for offline use. Its key-agreement methods do not provide forward secrecy because the receiver cannot contribute fresh key material during an exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: A COSE key states what type of key it is and can limit which algorithm or operations use it. An application must check those limits before using the key.

sections.title: Encoding Rules and Application Profiles
sections.content:
Cryptographic checks require both sides to use the same bytes. COSE therefore restricts encoding of the signature, encryption, and MAC input structures: encodings use definite lengths and the shortest possible argument length. An application must not create or process a map with a repeated label.

COSE defines security structures but does not require specific algorithms for every use. Each application profile selects its message types, headers, external-data encoding, required algorithms, and any method for discovering or negotiating those choices.

Applications that encrypt data also need to consider message length. The specification does not provide a uniform padding method, so an application may need its own rule to reduce what message size reveals.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need identical bytes for cryptographic checks, so COSE sets strict encoding rules. Each application must also choose which message types and algorithms it will accept.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect private keys. The RFC warns against using one key with different algorithms because doing so can expose information about the key. Applications should bind keys to their intended algorithms and check both the algorithm and key type.

Using the direct recipient method together with another recipient method can expose the direct key to another recipient, so COSE forbids that combination. The RFC also describes risks involving content keys shared between recipients and recommends adding key wrapping where needed to avoid implying proof of origin.

Before acting on a message, an application must decide whether the key owner is trusted and authorized for the requested action. Message length can reveal information, and applications are responsible for defining padding where needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications must protect private keys, check what each key is allowed to do, and decide whether the key owner is trusted. They should also consider whether message length reveals information.
